title: Developer Token Economics Simulator — Local Quickstart and Templates
author: Priya Menon
body:
Overview

This page describes the Developer Token Economics Simulator — a lightweight toolkit and set of templates that lets engineers model per-request and per-feature token costs for Redwood API calls in a local developer sandbox. The simulator helps teams estimate unit economics prior to production rollout, validate cost-related changes to prompts or batching strategies, and exercise quota/fallback policies in isolated environments.

When to use

- Planning: estimate monthly spend for feature launches based on expected request volumes and prompt length distributions.
- CI checks: add cost regressions to pre-merge checks to prevent accidental token regressions.
- Debugging: reproduce customer-reported high-cost patterns by replaying requests and inspecting token breakdowns.
- SDK tuning: test client-side bundling, prompt truncation, and streaming-to-batch tradeoffs.

Key features

- Pluggable price profiles (hosted, dedicated, committed-tier).
- Simulated batching and streaming models with configurable latency tradeoffs.
- Token attribution per request: system/instruction/user/content/embedding.
- Canary scenario runner for rollout experiments (A/B cost comparison).

Quickstart — run locally (10 minutes)

Prerequisites

1. Node 18+ or Python 3.10+.
2. Docker (optional, for reproducible runs).
3. Local copy of your reference prompt sets (see Files and templates).

Step 1 — clone the simulator templates

1. git clone git.example.com/internal/dev-token-econ-sim.git 
2. cd dev-token-econ-sim/templates/basic-quickstart

Step 2 — configure a price profile

Create config/prices.yaml with a profile for your intended deployment. Example: 

prices.yaml (example):

```
profiles:
  hosted_small:
    prompt_per_token_usd: 0.000004
    completion_per_token_usd: 0.000012
    embeddings_per_unit_usd: 0.0002
  dedicated_committed:
    prompt_per_token_usd: 0.0000025
    completion_per_token_usd: 0.0000075
    embeddings_per_unit_usd: 0.00015
```

Step 3 — provide a request sample set

Place a JSONL file at data/requests.jsonl where each line is a simple JSON object with keys: route, model, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, embeddings_count, and tags. Example line: 

```
{"route":"/v1/chat/completions","model":"redwood-large-1","prompt_tokens":320,"completion_tokens":120,"embeddings_count":0,"tags":["checkout","english"]}
```

Step 4 — run the simulator

- Node: npm run simulate -- --profile hosted_small --input data/requests.jsonl --output reports/hosted_small_report.csv
- Python: python simulate.py --profile hosted_small --input data/requests.jsonl --output reports/hosted_small_report.csv

The simulator will produce: a CSV with per-request token breakdown, aggregate cost summary, and a small JSON with percentile distributions (p50/p90/p99 prompt/completion tokens).

Files and templates included

- templates/basic-quickstart/ 
  - prices.yaml.example (price profile templates)
  - data/requests-sample.jsonl (sample requests for ecommerce and search features)
  - bin/run-local.sh (wrapper for common runs)
- templates/ci-check/ 
  - GitHub Actions workflow template for adding a cost gate in PRs (checks cost delta <= configured threshold)
- templates/canary/ 
  - ab-config.yaml (A/B test config: traffic split, profiles to compare)

Configuration table (recommended defaults)

| key | type | recommended example | notes |
|-----|------|---------------------|-------|
| profile | string | hosted_small | logical name used in CLI |
| prompt_per_token_usd | float | 0.000004 | vendor-specific published price |
| completion_per_token_usd | float | 0.000012 | often higher than prompt price |
| embeddings_per_unit_usd | float | 0.0002 | per embedding vector unit |
| batch_window_ms | int | 10 | simulates client batching window |
| streaming_penalty_ms | int | 20 | additional latency for streaming-to-batch conversion |

Example outputs

- reports/hosted_small_report.csv (columns: request_id, route, model, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, cost_usd, tags)
- reports/hosted_small_summary.json (p50/p90/p99 token stats and total cost)

Common support issues & canonical fixes

1) Discrepancy between local simulation and production billing
   - Symptom: simulated cost is significantly lower than billing.
   - Cause: production uses larger context windows or reference prompts not included in the simulation.
   - Fix: ensure request sample set includes pre-pended system instructions and real user context lengths. Update data/requests.jsonl to mirror production request envelope. See checklist below.

2) CI cost gate causing false positives on low-volume spikes
   - Symptom: PR blocked because cost delta > threshold from small sample noise.
   - Cause: PR sample set too small or not representative.
   - Fix: enlarge sample set to at least 500 requests or use percentile-based comparison (use p90 cost instead of mean). Update workflow to use templates/ci-check/github-actions-cost-gate.yaml.

3) Unexpectedly high embedding cost on hybrid features
   - Symptom: embedding spend dominates estimates for search-as-you-type features.
   - Cause: counting every preview query as full embedding.
   - Fix: instrument client to delay embeddings until a debounce window (example client change included in templates). Use embeddings_per_unit_usd from dedicated_committed profile to estimate committed-tier savings.

Checklist for accurate reproduction

- [ ] Include system prompts and metadata token counts in the sample lines.
- [ ] Mirror client-side bundling window and batch sizes.
- [ ] Represent expected user locale/tokenization differences (non-ASCII can change token counts).
- [ ] Verify price profile matches billing contract for the environment being simulated.

Adding a CI cost gate (example)

1. Copy templates/ci-check/github-actions-cost-gate.yaml to .github/workflows/
2. Update inputs: sample_path, baseline_report_artifact, cost_threshold_usd
3. The workflow will: run the simulator, upload the report, compare to baseline, and fail if delta > threshold.

Troubleshooting commands

- Run a single-sample run and view verbose token breakdown: 
  - python simulate.py --profile hosted_small --input data/requests.jsonl --single 42 --verbose
- Re-run with adjusted tokenization model: 
  - NODE_TOKENIZER_MODEL=gpt-tokenizer-v2 npm run simulate -- --profile hosted_small
